head: Craig's Structural Wall
Industry Failure Mode
How Neuren Solved It in PMS
rows: Underestimating true prevalence; failing to locate undiagnosed patients for trials and launch.
Co-funded a 2026 Mount Sinai / CureSHANK study (180k records) proving PMS occurs in 1 in 7,300 people—more than double prior 1-in-15,000 estimates.
Using generic scales that fail FDA review or drown drug signals in behavioral noise.
Aligned with FDA via Type C meetings on two bespoke co-primary endpoints (PMSA-C clinician scale & VABS-3 receptive communication).
Dilutive equity raises and unscalable small-batch manufacturing delays.
Locked in scalable oral liquid CMC early and self-funded Koala (~US$65M) via A$286.5M cash + ~US$91M–$93M 2026 trofinetide income.
Slow trial enrollment and payer pushback at launch due to weak community trust.
Deep strategic alliance with PMSF and CureSHANK (Presenting Sponsor at 2026 Family Conference; rapid Koala referral waitlists).

thesis.paragraph: Castle: a portable, low-cost brain scanner that can tell a bleed from a clot at the bedside or in an ambulance, where CT is not available — a genuinely new category. Moat: patents and know-how in electromagnetic imaging plus FDA De Novo status (first-of-kind clearance makes it the reference device). Lords: steady, grant-funded and frugal (~A$1.6m quarterly burn); raised A$14m in 2025 without heavy discounting. Misperception: the market treats it as a perennial 'next year' story; the pivotal trial is now ~80% enrolled at top US stroke centres. Odds against us: a medical-device adoption curve is slow and a further raise before revenue is likely. Device sleeve, not Insect: no earnings, so it cannot pass the Insect rules (PEG, 15% growth).
thesis.misperception: Trial will never finish. Evidence against: >230 of 300 enrolled at major US centres.
thesis.wrong: Trial misses its endpoints, FDA asks for a new study, or enrolment slips past mid-2027.
thesis.premortem: De Novo granted but hospitals don't buy (reimbursement), cash runs out, and a deep discounted raise follows.

thesis.paragraph: Castle: a faster version of a proven, generic drug — vardenafil as a nasal spray that is absorbed in ~10 minutes instead of ~60 — sold first through cash-pay channels (Australian Special Access, US telehealth) while it heads for full FDA approval on the cheaper 505(b)(2) route. Moat: formulation patents and know-how plus Aptar's device; full FDA approval would add a regulatory moat the compounded version lacks. Lords: founder-aligned (LTR Medical ~25%), frugal (A$1.6m quarterly burn), and quick at turning agreements into prescriptions; one ASX 'aware letter' in June 2026 is a governance point to watch. Misperception: the market prices it like a failed biotech (~A$60m EV) even though the drug is already approved molecule-wise, already selling in two countries, and the Phase III is a single study. Odds against us: ED is dominated by cheap generic pills, telehealth uptake is unproven, compounding rules could tighten, and a dilutive raise is likely in 2027.
thesis.misperception: Priced as a failed biotech, but the molecule is approved and the product is already being sold in Australia and the US.
thesis.wrong: US ROXUS prescriptions stay tiny through mid-2027, the FDA asks for more than one Phase III, or compounding rules shut the 503A channel.
thesis.premortem: Telehealth sales never take off, cash runs low, and a deeply discounted raise to fund Phase III halves the share price.

thesis.paragraph: Castle: Australia's property-settlement monopoly — almost every settlement runs through it. Moat: network effects and switching costs are real, and competition via interoperability was shelved. Lords: the CEO is cutting debt and has improved cash flow, but the UK keeps losing ~A$40m a year. Deep research changes the picture: the regulator is capping its prices (~16% cut from July 2027) and FY27 guidance has fallen to roughly break-even core profit. A regulated monopoly with falling earnings is a Turtle (or a Snake if the UK is fixed), not a Monkey. The market's pessimism is mostly justified for now — moved to the watch list.
thesis.misperception: Largely none today: the fall reflects real regulation and weaker property volumes. Possible future one: the UK option valued at zero.
thesis.wrong: (For a future buy) UK losses keep growing, or further fee cuts.
thesis.premortem: Buying a 'cheap monopoly' that the regulator keeps squeezing while UK losses continue.

thesis.paragraph: Castle: the world's largest copper producer and the lowest-cost major iron ore producer, with potash from mid-2027 — it stays profitable at the bottom of the cycle. Moat: low cost and scale. Lords: an internal CEO continuing a disciplined strategy; a very strong balance sheet. But FY26 earnings came from near-peak copper prices, and iron ore is sliding as Simandou ramps up. On my mid-cycle estimate BHP trades at ~9.5x EV / mid-cycle EBIT — above your ≤8x Bear rule. Not the cycle low yet. Bear entry: roughly A$38–43, or when iron-ore pessimism peaks.

thesis.wrong: Copper and iron ore fall together for years; Jansen keeps overrunning.
thesis.premortem: Bought in late 2026 thinking it was cheap, then iron ore fell to US$75 and copper corrected from its high.

facts: HY26 (to 30 Jun 2026): revenue A$2.89bn (−4.7%, Defence contract transition); EBITDA A$273.3m (+8.2%, record 9.4% margin); NPATA A$128.2m (+7.4%); EPS +14.4% helped by buy-backs.

9 Nov 2026: new CEO Mark Ralston (started 1 Sep) announced a simplification aiming for at least A$60m a year of cost savings by Dec 2027, ~A$30m one-off costs, and a weaker second-half revenue (telecoms and energy work deferred). FY26 NPATA growth guidance of 7–10% kept. Shares fell ~16% to a 52-week low.

thesis.paragraph: Castle: the maintenance contractor that keeps Australia's and New Zealand's defence bases, telecoms networks, water and roads running — boring, essential, recurring work on 5–10 year contracts with a 98% renewal rate. Moat: efficient scale and switching costs (customers rarely change who maintains critical assets mid-contract), plus defence security clearances that act like a licence. Lords: a brand-new CEO who did a 10-week review and came back with a cost-out plan, not an acquisition — a good sign of ability; capital returned through a large buy-back and fully franked dividends. Misperception: the market sold it 16% on a second-half revenue warning, but profit guidance was kept and the cost savings (A$60m a year ≈ 15% of NPATA) are not in anyone's numbers yet. At ~14.5x earnings with a ~4.7% fully franked yield, it is a Monkey at a fair-to-cheap price. Plain PEG (~1.45) fails our 1.2 rule; with the dividend added (Lynch's version) it is ~1.0.
thesis.misperception: A revenue dip in telecoms/energy means the business is shrinking. Evidence against: profit guidance kept, margins at a record, buy-back continuing, A$21bn work in hand.
thesis.wrong: FY26 NPATA misses the 7–10% guidance (Feb 2027), a major contract (Defence, Telstra) is lost, or cost savings slip past Dec 2027.
thesis.premortem: The new CEO's restructure disrupts operations, telecoms work stays deferred for years, and the P/E falls to ~11x while debt-funded acquisitions (e.g. Programmed) dilute returns.

castle.competitors: Downer, Service Stream, Programmed (for sale — both Ventia and Service Stream reportedly interested), CIMIC's UGL.
castle.climate: Government infrastructure and defence spending (tailwind), telco capex cycles (headwind now), wage inflation, interest rates.

Growth 10% = my estimate (NPATA growth + ~2–3% buy-back + cost-out). EBIT ~A$420m, net debt ~A$750m and FCF ~A$280m (cash conversion >90%) are my estimates — confirm in the FY26 annual report (Feb 2027). ROC ~20% estimated on equity + net debt.
